 Senate panel moves budget deadline to do tighter audit 
 Senate panel moves budget deadline to do tighter audit
 Local Politics 15 Nov 2026 • 12:14 AM MYT The Manila Times One of the longest-running English broadsheets in the Philippines
 THE Senate has moved the sponsorship of the proposed 2027 national budget committee report from Nov. 11 to Nov. 23 to conduct a strict line-by-line review of thousands of infrastructure projects.
 Senate Committee on Finance Chairman JV Ejercito said in a radio interview that the panel is auditing over 5,000 to 6,000 submissions from the House general appropriations bill alongside requests from various government agencies.
 Under stricter budget reforms, every project must now present a program of works, a certificate of implementability, geo-tagged coordinates, and regional or provincial development council approval.
 Ejercito noted that his office hired eight additional staff members to complete the verification process.
 Despite the adjusted schedule, he assured the public that plenary debates will immediately follow the Nov. 23 sponsorship to pass the spending measure before year-end and avoid a reenacted budget.
  The heightened scrutiny comes as lawmakers work to restore public trust following the flood control bribery scandal.
 Civil society organizations, the academe, and the People’s Budget Coalition have been invited to observe hearings and flag questionable entries.
  Addressing reports of farm-to-market road coordinates pointing to bodies of water like Benham Rise and the Celebes Sea, Ejercito said the committee is checking whether these were simple typographical errors while enforcing safeguards to eliminate double entries.
  Ejercito also emphasized the need to restore funding for foreign-assisted projects that were placed under unprogrammed appropriations by the House of Representatives. 
 Following a recent parliamentary visit to Japan — the country’s largest source of Official Development Assistance — Ejercito warned that delaying loan proceeds and government counterparts for flagship infrastructure could trigger costly commitment fees and hamper future loans.
  He is currently coordinating with the Department of Transportation (DOTr) and the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) to finalize exact figures for major projects, including the North-South Commuter Railway, Metro Manila Subway, Bataan-Cavite Interlink Bridge, and Laguna Lakeshore Highway.
 To accelerate sluggish economic growth — which recently dipped to 2 percent due to slow public spending — Ejercito urged lawmakers to balance local district projects with national infrastructure and industrial development.
 He also proposed shifting a portion of medical assistance funds like Maifip back to PhilHealth to strengthen universal health care and sustain zero-balance billing programs.
 Finally, Ejercito expressed hope that ongoing political noise and impeachment proceedings will soon conclude, warning that political division deters foreign investors while neighboring countries continue to outpace the Philippines in attracting capital.
 Hospital budgets slashed
 Meanwhile, Deputy Speaker Janette Garin said billions of pesos in proposed funding for hospital infrastructure, vaccines and health promotion were redirected to medical assistance in the House of Representatives’ proposed 2027 budget, citing low utilization and delays in government procurement to defend the realignment.
 Garin, a former health secretary, said Saturday that the changes were intended to ensure public funds reach patients instead of remaining unused because of bureaucratic bottlenecks.
 She cited the Health Facilities Enhancement Program, which recorded only 11 percent utilization during the period reviewed in congressional budget hearings. This prompted the House to reduce its proposed allocation by about P4.45 billion.
 Garin said the problem was not the need for health infrastructure but the DOH’s slow implementation of projects, with documents repeatedly passing between local governments, regional offices and the department’s central office.
 She also cited unspent allocations for pneumococcal vaccines for children in 2025 and 2026 to explain the roughly P4.87-billion reduction in proposed funding for family health, immunization and nutrition commodities.
 “The 2025 funds have not yet been used. The 2026 funds have not yet been used,” Garin said, adding that vaccine deliveries were expected to begin before the end of 2026 and continue throughout 2027.
 The House also reduced proposed health promotion funding by roughly P2 billion, with Garin questioning continued spending on television advertisements and printed materials that often went unused.
 She maintained that health information campaigns would continue under individual DOH programs, including those addressing hypertension and diabetes.
 Garin defended the transfer of funds to medical assistance, saying the arrangement would help patients settle hospital bills while giving hospitals resources for personnel, equipment and repairs.
 “Transferring the funds to the medical assistance program is actually hitting two birds with one stone. The money is being used to pay patients’ hospital bills,” she said.
 She rejected claims that the realignment would undermine public health services, saying the changes would make government spending more responsive to patients’ immediate needs.
 Garin urged the DOH to simplify its approval procedures to address delays in project implementation and improve budget utilization.
 “We are still waiting for the simplified guidelines so that documents will no longer be passed back and forth,” she said, expressing hope that the changes would take effect in 2027.
